subject: printing-press
title: Gutenberg's Startup: Combining Old Tech
summary: Gutenberg didn't invent the press, paper, or movable type. So what did he do?

keys.prompt: What did Gutenberg actually achieve if he didn't invent the parts?
keys.answer: He combined existing tech with his own inventions (a type mold, oil-based ink) into a system that could mass-produce books.

keys.prompt: Why did metal movable type take off faster in Europe than in China?
keys.answer: The Latin alphabet needs only a few dozen letters, so a full set of type cost far less than one for thousands of Chinese characters.

keys.prompt: How long did Gutenberg take from early evidence to his famous Bible, and what does that show?
keys.answer: About 15 years (a 1439 lawsuit to the 1454–56 Bible): big breakthroughs can need long R&D and outside money.

cards.title: He didn't invent the parts
cards.text: Screw presses were Roman. Movable type was first made in China. Paper and bound books existed already. So why do we remember Johann Gutenberg?

cards.question: Gutenberg didn't invent the press, paper or movable type. What do you think his real breakthrough was?

options.text: Inventing the first way to put ink on paper
Combining old and new tools into one system that could mass-produce books

cards.reveal: A system. He combined the screw press, movable type, the bound book and mill-made paper, then added his own hand mold for casting type and an oil-based ink.

cards.title: Combination innovation
cards.text: Around 1440, Gutenberg combined four existing technologies: the screw press, movable type, the bound book (codex), and mill-made paper. He added his own pieces too: a hand mold for casting metal letters and an oil-based ink that stuck to metal.
cards.example: Many startups work this way. The breakthrough is not one part. It is a system where all the parts finally work together.

cards.title: Asia got there first
cards.text: The Chinese artisan Bi Sheng made movable type from baked clay in the 11th century. The oldest surviving book printed with metal movable type is Korea's Jikji, from 1377.
cards.example: Chinese writing uses thousands of different characters, so a full set of type was very costly. The Latin alphabet needs only a few dozen letters, which made Gutenberg's system cheaper to set up.

why.q: Why would a few dozen letters make printing cheaper to set up?
why.a: A full set of type needs every character. Thousands of Chinese characters meant a huge, costly set; the Latin alphabet needed only a few dozen letters.

cards.title: Long R&D, outside money
cards.text: A 1439 lawsuit already describes Gutenberg's type, molds, and metals. His famous Bible came out between 1454 and 1456, published with his partner Johann Fust. That is about 15 years from early evidence to flagship product.
cards.example: More than 150 copies were printed. Only 20 complete copies survive intact today.

cards.title: Then it scaled
cards.text: By the end of the 1400s, around 270 European cities had printers. Between 1518 and 1520, printers handed out about 300,000 copies of Martin Luther's writings. Historians link printing to the Reformation and the Scientific Revolution.

cards.question: Books kept being copied by hand for centuries after printing arrived. Why do old methods hang on even after a better one shows up?
nudges: Think about cost, skills people already have, and trust.
Is there something today that is "better" but lots of people still do the old way?

questions.q: Why did metal movable type take off faster in Europe than in China?

options.text: The Latin alphabet has few letters, so a full set of type cost much less.
options.why: Right. Thousands of Chinese characters meant a huge, expensive set of type.
Bi Sheng made movable type in China in the 11th century, long before Gutenberg.
Woodblock printing on paper was the main method in East Asia, so paper was not the problem.

questions.q: Which of these was one of Gutenberg's own innovations?

options.text: A hand mold for casting metal type
options.why: Yes. That let him make lots of matching letters quickly.
Screw presses go back to the Romans. Farmers used them for grapes and olives.
The codex format also dates back to the Roman Empire.

questions.q: Which is the best summary of what Gutenberg achieved?

options.text: He combined old and new tools into a system that could mass-produce books.
options.why: Exactly. The system, not a single part, was the breakthrough.

options.text: He invented the first way to put ink on paper.
options.why: Woodblock printing had existed for centuries before him.

options.text: He made hand-copying disappear right away.
options.why: Books were still copied by hand for centuries afterward.

cards.prompt: Explain this to someone at dinner in 3 sentences.
starters: Gutenberg didn't invent every part, but…
His system worked well in Europe because…
